newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries revisit session lows at midday.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries revisit session lows at midday.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries revisited session lows at midday on Tuesday, weakened by a strong regional report on manufacturing, central bank selling and supply concerns, analysts said.
"Today we have an auction and supply is weighing on us," said Lee Youngdahl, bond market analyst at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co. Inc.
Traders said the Bundesbank was a seller of 10-year notes, adding some pressure to a market that opened lower in line with weakness in euro-government debt markets.
A market already wafting lower by mid-morning, was pushed to session lows by a strong report on manufacturing activity in the region of the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond.
The Richmond Fed March manufacturing shipments index rose to 29 in March from -10 in February. The new orders index also rose.
The Richmond Fed said its indices, which are coincident indicators, showed that the economy in the region was strong.
A 0.8 pct drop in the BOT/Mitsubishi index of adj U.S. retail sales for the week ended April 5 from the prior week was positive for the credit markets, but elicited no reaction.
The Treasury will sell $8.0 billion in 10-year Treasury Inflation Protected securities (TIPS) at 1300 EDT/1700 GMT.
Traders said there was not a great deal of interest evident in the securities before the auction but that that did not necessarily preclude a successful sale.

"I think it will go just fine," said Kevin Sluder, senior government trader at First Chicago Capital Markets, Inc. "(The inflation-indexed securities) are very much a portfolio investor type of vehicle for specific accounts like pension funds and tax-exempt accounts.
"There was not that much interest shown before the last auction (of inflation-indexed notes) but buyers showed up in droves at the auction," said Sluder.

Support from the dollar, whose recent sharp rise helped to lift the Treasury market on Monday, dissipated in morning trade on Tuesday and dealers took profits in the U.S. unit amid talk that the Bank of Japan might intervene to sell dollars for yen above 126.50.
The government reported that wholesale inventories were flat in February while wholesale sales jumped 2.1 percent after January's revised 0.8 pecent gain.
The wholesale sales increase was the biggest since a 2.7 percent rise in August 1994.

But analysts at MMS International said the potentially negative impact of that news on the bond market was offset by Challenger, Gray and Christmas Inc. report that job cuts rose 33.9 percent in March, the largest number since January 1996.
About 134,257 jobs were cut during the first quarter of 1997, 17 percent more than in the fourth quarter of 1996.
In early afternoon trade, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was down 14/32 to 94-02/32, yielding 7.11 percent.

Two-year notes were down 2/32 to 99-22/32, yielding 6.42 percent. In other key issues, the five-year note was down 6/32 to 99-14/32 to yield 6.76 percent, and the 10-year was down 10/32 to 95-13/32 to yield 6.90 percent.
Three-year bill rates were unchanged at 5.10 percent. Six-month and year-bill rates were up two basis points each to 5.33 percent and 5.36 percent, respectively.
